summary: Eritrea is one of the world's most closed destinations: virtually every nationality must obtain a visa in advance from an Eritrean embassy, approval can take weeks and is not guaranteed, and separate travel permits are required to leave Asmara.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months on arrival in Eritrea and have blank pages for the visa and stamps.

source.name: Ministry of Information of Eritrea — official government portal

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (yellow card)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers arriving from countries with a risk of yellow fever transmission.

source.name: Ministry of Information of Eritrea — official government portal

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not a formal requirement, but medical facilities are very limited, consular help is minimal and any serious case means evacuation abroad — comprehensive coverage including medical evacuation is essential in practice.

source.name: Ministry of Information of Eritrea — official government portal

onwardTicket.text: Embassies normally require a flight itinerary with the visa application, and you should hold a confirmed return or onward ticket when traveling.

source.name: Ministry of Information of Eritrea — official government portal

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; embassies may ask for evidence of funds or sponsorship with the visa application. Confirm requirements with the embassy before applying.

source.name: Ministry of Information of Eritrea — official government portal

currencyLimits.text: All foreign currency must be declared on the official form on arrival, money may only be exchanged through licensed channels (banks and Himbol offices), and exchange receipts should be kept — undeclared currency can be confiscated on departure.

source.name: Ministry of Information of Eritrea — official government portal

notes: Changing money on the black market is illegal and penalties are severe. Use only official exchange offices and keep every receipt.
Satellite phones and professional camera or communications equipment may require prior authorization. Check with the embassy before bringing them.

payments.text: Eritrea is effectively cash-only for foreigners. No ATMs accept international cards and card payments are essentially non-existent. Bring your entire budget in cash (US dollars or euros), declare it on arrival and exchange only through official channels.

safety.text: Day-to-day street crime in Asmara is low, but Eritrea is a tightly controlled state where several governments advise heightened caution or against non-essential travel: movement outside the capital requires permits, border areas with Ethiopia and Djibouti are militarised with landmine risks, communications are restricted and consular assistance is extremely limited.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Eritrea Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: October to March is the most comfortable window — highland Asmara is mild year-round thanks to its altitude, while the Red Sea coast around Massawa is only pleasant in these cooler months.

tips.text: A government travel permit is required to go anywhere outside Asmara, including Massawa and Keren. Apply several days ahead (tour operators can arrange it) and carry it at the frequent checkpoints.
Stay well away from the borders with Ethiopia and Djibouti. They are militarised, landmines remain from past conflicts, and foreigners have been detained in frontier zones.
Bring every dollar you will need in cash. There are no international ATMs, declare your money on arrival, exchange only through official channels and keep all receipts for departure.
Expect to be largely offline: internet access is slow and censored, mobile data for visitors is effectively unavailable, and SIM cards are very hard to obtain — tell people at home to expect silence.
Do not photograph government buildings, military sites, bridges or personnel — Asmara's modernist architecture is fine to shoot, but sensitive subjects can lead to detention.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Eritrea?
faq.answer: Yes — virtually every nationality needs a visa arranged in advance through an Eritrean embassy; there is no eVisa or visa on arrival. Apply well before your trip: processing regularly takes weeks, approval often depends on referral to Asmara, and it is not guaranteed.

faq.question: How long does an Eritrean visa take?
faq.answer: Allow at least several weeks. Applications are frequently referred to authorities in Asmara for approval, and many travelers apply one to two months ahead. Using an Eritrean tour operator as sponsor can smooth the process. Confirm requirements with the embassy handling your application.

faq.question: Can I travel outside Asmara in Eritrea?
faq.answer: Only with a travel permit issued by the authorities in Asmara. This applies to Massawa, Keren, the Dahlak islands and everywhere else outside the capital. Permits take several days, name the specific places you may visit, and are checked at road checkpoints.

faq.question: Can I use cards or ATMs in Eritrea?
faq.answer: No — international cards do not work anywhere. Bring your whole budget in cash (US dollars or euros), declare it on the currency form on arrival, exchange only at banks or official Himbol offices, and keep the receipts, which can be checked when you leave.

faq.question: Is Eritrea safe to visit?
faq.answer: Street crime in Asmara is rare, but the wider picture demands caution: several governments advise against non-essential travel, border zones are militarised with landmine risks, movement is controlled by permits, communications are restricted and consular help is extremely limited. Travel with a reputable operator and follow the rules precisely.
